title: Host-plant nitrogen preference did not predict faster butterfly gains at higher nitrogen deposition on 3,409 British transects in 1985-2024
abstract: We tested whether butterfly species whose larval host plants prefer nitrogen-rich soils increased relative to species of poor-soil hosts at sites with more atmospheric nitrogen deposition. We used 507,113 UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme site indices of 54 resident taxa on 3,409 transects in England, Wales and Scotland from 1985 to 2024. Host N was the mean British Ellenberg N value of primary host plants. Site deposition was the 1986-2012 mean CBED total N deposition for the 5-km square. Site x year, species x year and site x species fixed effects compared species at the same site in the same year. The host N x deposition x decade term was negative, not positive as predicted: -0.0118 log units per decade per SD x SD with trait, thermal-niche and geography controls (95% CI -0.0253 to +0.0017; 50-km clusters). This excludes a relative gain larger than about 6% over 40 years for host N 8 versus 2 at 10 kg N/ha/yr more deposition. A 10,000-shuffle trait permutation gave one-sided p = 0.97 for the predicted sign. With controls, only 1 of 6 region-period samples was positive (northern England 1985-2004). A community host-N index did not increase at low, mid or high deposition. A positive control (species thermal index x site northing) was detected (+0.104, SE 0.045). An exploratory split into ammonia (NHx) and oxidised N (NOx) gave opposite signs, but these became small with controls and did not replicate across regions and periods. Limitations: modelled 5-km deposition, no land-cover data, literature host lists and recorder-chosen sites.

display.caption: a: UKBMS transects and mean 1986-2012 CBED total N deposition. b: Host-N x deposition x decade coefficient by region and period, without and with trait and climate controls (95% CI, 50-km clusters); the eutrophication hypothesis predicts values above zero. c: Host-N trend slope by site deposition decile, relative to the lowest decile. d: Community host-plant N index by deposition tercile (site fixed effects; change from 1985).

a: Within-site national trend of each species against host-plant Ellenberg N. b: Primary coefficient against 10,000 shuffles of host N among species. c: Sensitivity estimates of the host-N x deposition term and the positive control (species thermal index x northing).

Exploratory: host N x NHx and host N x NOx terms in a joint model, without (a) and with (b) trait and geography controls, by region and period (95% CI). The pooled split shrinks with controls and changes sign in northern England after 2004.
